answers.explanation: 32 bits gives 2³² ≈ 4.3 billion addresses, which seemed endless in 1981.
2¹²⁸ is about 3.4 × 10³⁸ addresses, enough to give every device its own public address.
The central pool ran out in 2011, and the regional registries ran out over the following years.
On a log scale each step up the axis is ×10, so steady exponential growth looks like a straight line.
Once millions of devices speak a protocol, you can't just change it. Old systems stay in service for decades.
The early Internet assumed every host was run by a trusted researcher. Security has been added on top ever since.
IPv6 has no broadcast. It uses multicast, addressing just the group of hosts that care.
Routers can use the flow label to give every packet in a stream consistent treatment.
A simple fixed-size main header is faster for routers, and new extension headers can be added later.
The router announces the prefix, and the host fills in the rest. That also makes moving a whole network to a new prefix easier.
